visual.pie: Nature of business · four sectors · entrepreneurship · start-up challenges and opportunities

turnos.t: Now, unit one point one: what is a business?
On the poster, this box lists the nature of business, the four sectors, entrepreneurship, and start-up challenges and opportunities.
Start with the definition.
A business is an organization that uses resources, called inputs, to produce goods or services, called outputs, that satisfy customers' needs and wants.
Look around you: your clothes, your phone, your lunch.
Almost all of it was designed, made and delivered by businesses.
The course also has four key concepts, and they all start here: sustainability, ethics, change and creativity.
Businesses must meet human needs while protecting the planet.
Your notes picture this with Kate Raworth's Doughnut model: an inner ring of human needs, the social foundation, and an outer ring of planetary boundaries, the ecological ceiling.
The goal is the safe space in between.

visual.nota: Feedback: an output becomes an input to the same system

turnos.t: Your notes describe a business as a system: inputs, processes, outputs and feedback.
Inputs are the resources needed to create a product: physical, like raw materials and machines; financial, the funds to set up and run the business; and human.
Economics calls them the four factors of production.
Land: natural resources, like coffee beans.
Labour: human effort, the baristas.
Capital: man-made tools, like the espresso machine.
And enterprise: the initiative and risk-taking that combines the other three.
So which factor carries the risk? Enterprise.
Outputs are goods, which are tangible, like a cupcake, or services, which are intangible, like a concert.
A restaurant sells both.
And feedback is when an output becomes an input again, like customer comments that improve the product.

tarjetas.detalle: Right number of skilled staff, treated ethically · hiring baristas
Enough money over time · cash for the espresso machine
Right product, price, time, customers · loyalty card
How the core activity is done · brewing speed, stock

turnos.t: The processes are grouped into four business functions, and every business has them, even a one-person café.
Human resources management makes sure the business employs the right number of skilled employees, treated ethically and within the law: hiring and training baristas.
Finance and accounts make sure there is enough money to keep operating over time.
Marketing means selling the right product, at the right price, at the right time, to the right customers.
And remember: the customer buys the product, the consumer uses it.
A parent buying a toy is the customer; the child is the consumer.
Operations is how the core activity is carried out, and in what quantity.
The four depend on each other, which is why the course has one unit for each.

visual.titulo: Added value in one cup of coffee (illustrative)

turnos.t: Why does a business exist?
Because it adds value.
Added value is the difference between the price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and services used to make it.
A café buys beans and milk for about forty cents a cup and sells the coffee for two euros twenty.
The added value is one euro eighty.
At two hundred cups a day, that is three hundred and sixty euros per day.
But careful: added value is not profit.
Wages and rent are still paid from it, so a business can add a lot of value and still make a loss.
How do you add value?
Through branding, convenience, quality, design or service.

visual.titulo: The four sectors, with Spanish examples

turnos.t: Now the sectors of the economy.
The primary sector extracts raw materials from the Earth: farming, fishing, forestry, mining and drilling.
The secondary sector manufactures and processes them into products, and includes construction.
The tertiary sector sells services: shops, banks, healthcare, transport.
The quaternary sector is based on knowledge and information: research, information technology, data and web services.
Some experts still count it inside the tertiary sector.
Most products pass through several sectors, a chain of production.
A chair: timber is harvested, primary; designed with software, quaternary; made, secondary; sold in a shop, tertiary.
A business in two or more sectors is integrated, like a farm selling tomatoes in its own shop: primary and tertiary.

visual.titulo: Spain: % of total employment, 1991 vs 2023 (World Bank)

turnos.t: Over time, the sectors change size.
This is structural change: a shift in the relative size of the sectors in an economy.
As countries develop, work moves from primary to secondary, then to tertiary and quaternary.
Spain shows it clearly.
In nineteen ninety-one the tertiary sector had fifty-seven point three percent of jobs; in twenty twenty-three, seventy-six point five.
The secondary sector fell from thirty-two to twenty percent: from one job in three to one in five.
The primary sector fell from ten point six to three point five. Why?
Rising incomes mean more spending on services.
Technology means fewer workers on farms and in factories.
And globalisation moves manufacturing to lower-cost countries.
When factories close, their suppliers lose orders and workers need retraining.
An entrepreneur is a person who creates and manages a new business, taking on financial risk in the hope of making a profit.
An intrapreneur shows the same creativity inside an existing organization, so the employer carries the risk.
Sara, who leaves her job to open a coffee shop, is an entrepreneur.
A barista at a coffee chain who suggests a new oat-milk drink, which the chain then launches, is an intrapreneur.
Why do people start a business?
Your notes give seven reasons: a new idea, a passion to make change, a market need, earning a living, greater financial reward, more control, and a better work-life balance.
In very low-income countries, many start out of necessity, because there are few jobs.

visual.pie: A speciality coffee shop: the kind of start-up in the Sara case (invented)

turnos.t: Here is the case from the app.
Sara has saved fifteen thousand euros, but the premises and the espresso machine cost forty thousand.
Two well-known coffee chains are on her street.
She was a barista for six years, but has never managed a business.
The most common challenge is lack of funds.
With no trading record, a bank sees her as risky, and may refuse the twenty-five thousand euro loan or charge high interest.
Then strong competition: the chains have loyal customers and lower costs.
Others are a market that is too small, unskilled staff, poor management skills, and economic or political shocks.
But a start-up also has opportunities: it is flexible and personal, can serve a niche the chains ignore, and can use cheap technology like social media.

filas: What do we want to achieve?
How will we produce it, with whom?

turnos.t: Sara's next step is a business plan: a document that sets out a new business's objectives, and the strategies and resources it will use to achieve them, often to obtain finance.
It covers the product, market research, marketing, operations and people, and financial forecasts such as a cash-flow forecast.
Your notes add Simon Sinek's Golden Circle: the why comes first, then the how and the what.
A good plan is a story supported by evidence.
Why does it help?
It gives the entrepreneur credibility, reduces risk, and shows the bank the loan can be repaid.
The steps to start up: refine the idea, write the plan, choose a legal structure, register, find a location, hire staff, and get funding.

turnos.t: Let's close one point one with the exam.
'Define entrepreneur', two marks: the definition, plus a detail or an example.
'With reference to the data, describe the change in Spain's employment structure', four marks: a figure for each sector, then the overall pattern.
A vague answer like 'more services, less industry' gets one.
'Distinguish between an entrepreneur and an intrapreneur': compare the same aspect, who carries the risk.
'Explain two challenges Sara may face', four marks: twice, identify and explain, with her numbers.
And 'explain how a business plan could help Sara get a loan': the forecasts show she can repay, so the bank sees less risk.
Next: one point two, the types of business entities.
